paragraphs: Automatically assessing a painting requires examples that describe aesthetic qualities beyond a single overall score. This paper addresses the scarcity of richly annotated artistic image datasets. Its APDD collection covers 24 artistic categories and 10 aesthetic attributes, providing several dimensions through which models can learn to assess paintings and drawings.

APDDv2 expands the image collection and improves annotation quality relative to the first version. It also adds detailed language comments alongside the artist-labeled assessments. These comments provide descriptive information that numerical scores alone cannot express, making the dataset useful for studying both aesthetic ratings and the language used to explain artistic judgments.

The paper also introduces an updated ArtCLIP assessment model for specific painting styles. Experiments report better aesthetic evaluation accuracy and efficacy than its predecessor. The contribution therefore combines improved training and evaluation material with a revised model, showing how richer artistic annotations can support the development of automatic assessment systems.
neurips-2024-apddv2-aesthetics-of-painti.tldr: APDDv2 expands artist-annotated painting data with richer comments and introduces an improved ArtCLIP aesthetic assessment model.

paragraphs: Object-centric learning tries to discover individual objects in images without manual supervision. Many approaches build object representations by gathering visual features that resemble one another. This becomes difficult when different parts of the same object have very different appearances: visual similarity alone may provide an incomplete basis for deciding which features belong together.

The paper adds a top-down pathway that uses the model’s developing interpretation of an object to guide feature processing. It first builds an initial estimate of the object’s semantics, then adjusts the model to emphasize features relevant to that estimate. The model therefore uses its own output as a signal for improving the representation it constructs.

This self-modulation connects object interpretation with feature selection, addressing the mismatch between internally varied objects and grouping based on homogeneous features. The authors report state-of-the-art results across multiple synthetic and real-world object-discovery benchmarks. These findings support the value of adding semantic feedback to unsupervised object representation learning.
neurips-2024-bootstrapping-top-down-info.tldr: A top-down feedback pathway uses a model’s own object interpretations to improve unsupervised object discovery.

paragraphs: Split federated learning distributes a model across clients and a main server. Clients train their portion in parallel through federated learning, while the server trains the remaining portion. Understanding whether this arrangement converges is challenging because client and server updates can proceed at different paces, especially when clients hold different data distributions.

The paper develops convergence analysis for this setting with heterogeneous data. For strongly convex objectives, it establishes a rate of O(1/T); for general convex objectives, the rate is O(1/T^(1/3)), where T counts training rounds. These rates describe how the theoretical convergence bounds improve as training continues within the respective objective classes.

The analysis also extends to non-convex objectives and training with unavailable clients. Numerical experiments support the theoretical results and show better performance than federated learning and split learning when many clients have highly heterogeneous data. That empirical comparison is tied to the stated setting, while the central contribution supplies a theoretical foundation for analyzing split federated training.
neurips-2024-convergence-analysis-of-spl.tldr: The paper establishes convergence rates for split federated learning and extends its analysis to non-convex objectives and unavailable clients.

paragraphs: Approximate nearest neighbor search finds data points close to a query while avoiding the work of an exhaustive search. Leading graph-based methods connect nearby points and explore this graph through greedy beam search. A large graph can nevertheless send the search through many points that contribute little to finding useful neighbors.

CSPG reorganizes this process by randomly dividing the dataset into partitions and building a smaller, sparse proximity graph within each one. Routing vectors connect the partitions. Search then proceeds through two stages: quickly approaching relevant regions and expanding across partitions. This structure gives the algorithm a way to navigate between smaller graphs while limiting unnecessary exploration.

The authors theoretically show that CSPG can accelerate existing graph-based search algorithms by reducing such exploration. Benchmark experiments report query-throughput improvements of 1.5 to 2 times at almost all tested recall levels. Recall reflects how many desired neighbors are recovered, so the results indicate faster search across a broad range of tested retrieval-quality settings.
neurips-2024-cspg-crossing-sparse-proxim.tldr: CSPG accelerates graph-based nearest neighbor search with sparse partition graphs and routing, reporting 1.5–2× query-throughput gains.

paragraphs: Domain adaptive object detection transfers a detector from a labeled source domain to a target domain without labels. Pretrained vision-language models supply general visual knowledge, and adapters can learn features shared across domains while keeping the visual encoder frozen. The paper argues that a domain-agnostic adapter remains biased toward the source and can discard information useful for distinguishing target-domain objects.

DA-Ada separates adaptation into two complementary components. The Domain-Invariant Adapter learns knowledge that transfers across domains. The Domain-Specific Adapter injects domain-specific information from what the visual encoder discards. Together, they aim to retain useful target-domain distinctions alongside the general knowledge and shared features that support transfer.

The approach matters because successful adaptation may require preserving differences as well as finding similarities. Experiments across multiple domain adaptive detection tasks show that DA-Ada can efficiently produce a domain-aware visual encoder that improves detection. The reported findings support combining shared and domain-specific knowledge when adapting to an unlabeled target.
neurips-2024-da-ada-learning-domain-awar.tldr: DA-Ada combines shared and domain-specific adapters to improve object detection in unlabeled target domains.

paragraphs: A 3D detector must estimate where an object is and how a bounding box should fit around it. Models can lose localization accuracy when deployed with different sensor setups or in different geographic locations. DiffuBox addresses this domain-shift problem by refining a detector’s coarse box using the surrounding LiDAR measurements.

The proposed refinement method uses a domain-agnostic diffusion model conditioned on points near the initial bounding box. It adjusts the box’s location, size, and orientation together. This makes local point information central to the correction process and treats several aspects of box geometry as parts of the same refinement task.

The authors evaluate the method under several domain adaptation settings and report significant improvements across datasets, object classes, and detectors. This breadth suggests that the refinement approach can help beyond a single tested detector or category. Its stated contribution is better localization under domain changes, using an existing coarse detection and nearby LiDAR points as the basis for correction.
neurips-2024-diffubox-refining-3d-object.tldr: DiffuBox uses nearby LiDAR points and a diffusion model to refine 3D bounding boxes under domain shift.

paragraphs: Fine-tuning a text-to-image diffusion model on a few personal images can make it reproduce a particular subject or style. However, the customized model may struggle to combine that subject with pretrained concepts or with another customization. This paper addresses the loss of compositional flexibility that can accompany faithful personalization.

Direct Consistency Optimization changes the fine-tuning objective to control deviation from the pretrained model. The aim is to retain pretrained knowledge while learning the customization. Experiments report a better trade-off between subject or style consistency and alignment with the text prompt than previous baselines, including stronger reference fidelity than fine-tuning with an additional prior dataset.

The authors also demonstrate merging separately customized subject and style models without interference, enabling their subjects and styles to be composed. In the reported comparisons, this approach improves prompt and subject fidelity over methods that optimize ordinary fine-tuned models afterward for merging. The findings connect preservation during training with more useful composition after customization.
neurips-2024-direct-consistency-optimiza.tldr: Direct Consistency Optimization preserves pretrained knowledge during customization, improving prompt alignment, reference fidelity, and subject–style model composition.

paragraphs: Continuous graph neural networks describe changes in node features through differential equations. Traditional versions use either ordinary integer-order derivatives or a single fractional derivative order. DRAGON broadens this design by learning a probability distribution over derivative orders, allowing multiple kinds of feature-update dynamics to contribute within one framework.

The distribution determines how different derivative orders are combined. This gives the model flexibility beyond committing to one order throughout its dynamics. The authors interpret the resulting behavior through a non-Markovian random walk on a graph, where feature evolution involves history, together with an anomalous diffusion process governing how information spreads.

This interpretation links the mathematical construction to the way node features change and interact over a graph. Empirical evaluations cover a range of graph learning tasks and consistently report better performance than traditional continuous graph neural networks. The findings support learning the mixture of derivative orders as a useful way to represent complex graph dynamics.
neurips-2024-distributed-order-fractiona.tldr: DRAGON learns a distribution over fractional derivative orders to model richer graph dynamics and improve graph learning performance.

paragraphs: Multi-view subspace clustering groups observations using several representations of the same data. Tensor-based approaches capture relationships across those views, but existing methods can be expensive, depend heavily on complete dictionaries, and lose local geometric information. The paper also identifies a problem with treating all tensor singular values equally when some are associated with noise.

STONE addresses these issues through three connected changes. An enhanced anchor dictionary mechanism recovers a low-rank anchor structure, reducing computation and improving resilience when dictionaries are inadequate. An anchor hypergraph Laplacian regularizer preserves the data’s geometry within the learned subspace representation, helping retain relationships that a purely global representation can overlook.

The third component uses an improved hyperbolic tangent function to approximate tensor rank while accounting for differences among singular values. Together, these changes improve the dictionary, geometric structure, and tensor representation. Experiments across several datasets report better clustering effectiveness and efficiency than state-of-the-art methods, supporting the combined framework’s scalability and representation quality.
neurips-2024-from-dictionary-to-tensor-a.tldr: STONE improves multi-view clustering through anchor dictionary learning, geometry preservation, and a more discriminating tensor-rank approximation.

paragraphs: Disentangled representation learning seeks to separate observations into underlying factors that make data easier to understand and generate. Many methods assume these semantic factors are statistically independent. This paper addresses situations where meaningful factors are correlated, so separating them should also preserve an account of how they relate to one another.

The proposed framework represents factors and their relationships in a bidirectional weighted graph. A beta-VAE module extracts factors that become the initial graph nodes. A multimodal large language model then discovers and ranks latent correlations, updating the edge weights. The two modules provide complementary information: candidate attributes and estimates of their interrelationships.

This design makes factorization and relationship modeling part of the same unsupervised system. Experiments report superior disentanglement and reconstruction performance, alongside enhanced interpretability and generalizability inherited from the multimodal language model. The central idea is that useful factor representations can distinguish attributes while explicitly describing correlations, instead of relying on statistical independence.
neurips-2024-graph-based-unsupervised-di.tldr: A beta-VAE and multimodal language model jointly learn separate attributes and a weighted graph of their correlations.

paragraphs: Video sentiment analysis often studies emotions expressed by people appearing in a video. This paper instead examines viewers’ reactions through the comments they leave. It introduces a task for inferring opinions and emotions in responses to micro videos, with potential applications in understanding public reactions and assessing advertising effectiveness.

To support the task, the authors manually annotate CSMV, a dataset containing 107,267 comments and 8,210 micro videos spanning 68.83 hours. They describe it as the largest video multimodal sentiment dataset by scale and duration to their knowledge. The paired video-and-comment setting provides material for studying responses in relation to the content that prompted them.

The proposed baseline, VC-CSA, uses video content when analyzing comment sentiment. This connects the interpretation of a response to the video it addresses. Experiments report significant improvements over established baselines, supporting the value of video-aware analysis for this task. The contribution combines a new research target, annotated data, and a method for using the relevant multimodal context.
neurips-2024-infer-induced-sentiment-of-.tldr: The paper introduces a video-comment sentiment task, a large annotated dataset, and a baseline that uses video content to interpret viewer reactions.

paragraphs: Mechanical structures generate and transmit noise through vibration, so predicting vibration helps guide noise reduction. Numerical simulations can be expensive, while learned surrogate models offer much faster evaluation with an accuracy trade-off. This paper creates a benchmark for measuring that trade-off in plates subjected to harmonic excitation.

The dataset contains 12,000 plate geometries and their numerical solutions. It varies beadings, material, boundary conditions, load position, and sizes, providing different structural and loading configurations. The proposed network predicts vibration patterns for a plate at a specified excitation frequency, combining operator-learning principles with implicit models for encoding shape.

The architecture is designed to handle the highly variable frequency responses found in dynamic systems. The authors introduce evaluation metrics and compare the method with DeepONets, Fourier Neural Operators, and more traditional neural networks, reporting better performance on their benchmark. They also state that the method can support design optimization, connecting the prediction task to the practical search for improved structures.
neurips-2024-learning-to-predict-structu.tldr: A 12,000-geometry benchmark and a new learning architecture advance fast prediction of frequency-dependent plate vibrations.

paragraphs: A multimodal language model’s image understanding depends heavily on its visual encoder. The authors find that no single encoder dominates across different image content: an encoder effective for general images may perform poorly on documents or charts. MoVA addresses this uneven expertise by selecting and combining multiple vision experts according to the current task.

Its coarse stage routes inputs to suitable experts using the user’s instruction, the image, and information about each expert’s capabilities. A language model helps interpret which experts fit that context. The fine stage then uses a mixture-of-vision-expert adapter to extract and fuse task-specific knowledge from the selected representations.

The two stages connect choosing relevant expertise with combining the information it provides. This makes visual processing responsive to multimodal context rather than dependent on one encoder’s strengths across every input. Experiments report significant gains over state-of-the-art methods on a wide range of challenging multimodal benchmarks, supporting the effectiveness and generalization benefits of the approach.
neurips-2024-mova-adapting-mixture-of-vi.tldr: MoVA selects and fuses vision experts according to the image, user instruction, and each expert’s capabilities.

paragraphs: Neural surface reconstruction can represent geometry through a signed distance function and recover it using volume rendering. Although this approach is powerful, it can miss fine geometric structures and produce visible defects. The paper compares it with density-based rendering to identify where its optimization becomes difficult.

The authors identify two contributing factors: converting the signed distance representation into density and applying geometric regularization. NeuRodin addresses these issues through a two-stage framework intended to combine high-fidelity surfaces with the optimization flexibility of density-based methods. Its strategies support changes in arbitrary topology and reduce artifacts associated with density bias.

The method is evaluated on Tanks and Temples and ScanNet++, using only RGB images with known camera poses. The reported results show superior reconstruction and strong performance in both indoor and outdoor environments. The contribution is therefore both diagnostic and methodological: it identifies sources of surface degradation and introduces a reconstruction framework designed to improve the resulting geometry.
neurips-2024-neurodin-a-two-stage-framew.tldr: NeuRodin uses a two-stage reconstruction framework to improve geometric detail and reduce artifacts from posed RGB images.

paragraphs: A sparse function, or junta, depends on only a subset of its input variables. This paper studies the difficulty of identifying that subset through gradient-based learning. It introduces Differentiable Learning Queries, a statistical-query framework that models gradient information for a chosen loss function and an arbitrary model.

For generic product distributions, the authors give a tight characterization of the query complexity of learning the relevant variables. The loss function is decisive. With squared loss, differentiable queries match correlation statistical queries, which can be substantially less powerful than general statistical queries. With other simple losses, including absolute-error loss, they match the complexity of general statistical queries within this setting.

The authors also provide evidence that this framework captures actual gradient learning. It correctly describes learning complexity for a two-layer neural network in the mean-field regime and linear scaling. These results show how the loss can alter the information available for learning sparse structure, while grounding the query analysis in a specified neural-network regime.
neurips-2024-on-the-complexity-of-learni.tldr: A new gradient-query framework shows that the chosen loss can sharply change the complexity of identifying a sparse function’s relevant inputs.

paragraphs: Offline policy evaluation estimates how a new sequential decision policy would perform using interactions recorded under other policies. Such estimates matter when trying a policy directly could be costly or unsafe. Many estimators are available, but choosing the most suitable one for a particular dataset and application remains difficult.

OPERA addresses this choice by adaptively blending several estimators. It uses a statistical procedure to determine the combination from the available dataset, avoiding an explicit selection of a single estimator. The framework is estimator-agnostic, so its central contribution concerns how estimates are combined rather than requiring one particular evaluation method.

The authors prove consistency and additional desirable policy-evaluation properties for their combined estimator. They also demonstrate that it can select higher-performing policies than alternative approaches in healthcare and robotics. These results connect a theoretical property of the estimate with a practical decision: choosing which policy to use. The broader aim is to make offline evaluation easier to apply across tasks.
neurips-2024-opera-automatic-offline-pol.tldr: OPERA adaptively combines offline policy estimators and improves policy selection in reported healthcare and robotics evaluations.

paragraphs: Privacy risks from language models extend beyond revealing information encountered during training. Models may also infer personal attributes from newly supplied content. This paper asks whether vision-language models can make such inferences from apparently benign images posted online, expanding the question from text to visual material.

The authors build an image dataset with human-annotated labels for personal attributes of the image owners. They deliberately use images where the relevant private information does not come from direct depictions of people. This design examines what models can infer from other visual clues, beyond traditional recognition of attributes from a person’s appearance.

Across seven state-of-the-art vision-language models, the study finds accuracy reaching 77.6% for personal-attribute inference. It also observes that inference accuracy increases with general model capability. This pattern suggests that future, more capable models could become stronger tools for privacy-infringing inference. The findings motivate defenses addressing what images reveal indirectly, alongside protections against leakage of training data.
neurips-2024-private-attribute-inference.tldr: Vision-language models infer owners’ private attributes from images without direct human depictions, reaching up to 77.6% accuracy in the study.

paragraphs: Language-model agents face enormous action spaces because each action can consist of many possible token sequences. Prior approaches constrain available actions using human knowledge, but they also miss opportunities to assign learning credit to individual tokens. This paper studies how token-level optimization can provide finer supervision without requiring a restricted action set.

Simply flattening actions into a token sequence introduces discrepancies relative to action-level optimization. The authors analyze these differences and derive Bellman backup with Action Decomposition, or BAD, to account for credit both within actions and between actions. This preserves the relationship between tokens that form an action and the larger sequence of environmental decisions.

Integrating BAD into PPO produces Policy Optimization with Action Decomposition, or POAD. The method combines finer credit assignment with lower optimization complexity. Evaluations across diverse interactive testbeds support improved learning efficiency and generalization, as well as the theoretical analysis. The contribution makes token-level learning consistent with the decision structure the agent is meant to optimize.
neurips-2024-reinforcing-llm-agents-via-.tldr: POAD improves language-agent reinforcement learning by assigning token-level credit while preserving dependencies within and between actions.

paragraphs: Continual learning trains a model through a sequence of tasks whose data distributions can change. Saliency-driven Experience Replay, or SER, uses ideas from human visual attention to guide this process. Its biological motivation concerns the role of early visual processing and persistent saliency biases in how the brain handles visual information.

The method uses features from an auxiliary saliency prediction task as a modulation signal for classification learning. These features guide and stabilize training across the changing task sequence. The central idea is to make information about visually salient content influence how the classifier learns, bringing an additional source of structure into continual learning.

Experiments show improvements to state-of-the-art continual learning methods in both class-incremental and task-incremental settings, with gains reaching about twenty percentage points in some cases. The learned features are also more robust to spurious features and adversarial attacks than baseline methods. These findings link saliency-based modulation with both better sequential learning performance and improved robustness in the tested settings.
neurips-2024-saliency-driven-experience-.tldr: SER uses saliency prediction features to improve continual classification learning and robustness, with gains of about twenty percentage points in some cases.

paragraphs: Unpaired data translation requires mapping between distributions without matched examples specifying each desired transformation. Optimal transport offers a principled way to construct such mappings. The paper focuses on the Schrödinger bridge, a dynamic, entropy-regularized version of optimal transport, and the computational burden of existing approaches for high-dimensional data.

Existing methods can require fully training a diffusion-type model at every iteration or use mini-batch approximations that introduce substantial errors. The proposed algorithm avoids training multiple diffusion-type models. It arises by discretizing a flow of path measures, meaning that the mathematical object being updated describes distributions over entire transformation trajectories.

The authors show that the Schrödinger bridge is the only stationary point of this flow. That property identifies the intended equilibrium of the construction without itself asserting that every discretized run reaches it. The paper demonstrates the algorithm on several unpaired translation tasks, connecting the mathematical framework with practical transformations between data distributions.
neurips-2024-schrodinger-bridge-flow-for.tldr: Schrödinger Bridge Flow supports unpaired data translation without repeatedly training multiple diffusion-type models.

paragraphs: Video diffusion models generate detailed videos through repeated denoising steps, but those repeated passes make sampling computationally expensive. SF-V targets this bottleneck by adapting a pretrained video diffusion model to generate a video in a single forward pass. The goal is to preserve useful video quality while sharply reducing denoising work.

The approach uses adversarial training to fine-tune Stable Video Diffusion. The resulting model captures both spatial dependencies within frames and temporal dependencies across frames in its single-step output. This matters because shortening generation must still account for the structure of individual images and the relationships that make them form a coherent video.

Experiments report competitive generation quality with about a 23-fold denoising speedup over Stable Video Diffusion. Against existing works, the abstract reports approximately sixfold speedup with better generation quality. These findings establish a substantially faster generation approach in the evaluated settings and suggest a route toward real-time video synthesis and editing.
neurips-2024-sf-v-single-forward-video-g.tldr: SF-V uses adversarial fine-tuning for single-pass video generation, reporting roughly 23× faster denoising than Stable Video Diffusion.

paragraphs: Masked diffusion generates discrete data by learning to recover information hidden through masking. This paper argues that unnecessarily complicated formulations have obscured its training objective and encouraged suboptimal design choices. It develops a simpler framework that connects existing perspectives and supports a broader class of masking processes.

The key theoretical result expresses the continuous-time variational objective as a weighted integral of cross-entropy losses. This makes the training target easier to interpret in terms of prediction losses. The framework also allows state-dependent masking schedules, extending how masking can vary with the data state during the process.

At GPT-2 scale, models trained on OpenWebText outperform prior diffusion language models by perplexity and lead on four of five zero-shot language modeling tasks. For pixel-level image modeling, the reported results are 2.75 bits per dimension on CIFAR-10 and 3.40 on ImageNet 64×64, outperforming previous discrete diffusion methods and similarly sized autoregressive models. The results connect the simplified formulation with stronger discrete generative modeling.
neurips-2024-simplified-and-generalized-.tldr: A simpler masked-diffusion objective supports generalized masking schedules and improves reported language and pixel-level image modeling results.

paragraphs: Language models can encounter incompatible information in retrieved material and in knowledge encoded during training. Such conflicts contribute to hallucinations, yet studying only disagreement between a model and an external passage leaves other conflict patterns unexplored. ConflictBank provides a benchmark for examining these patterns more comprehensively.

The benchmark contains 7.45 million claim-evidence pairs and 553,000 question-answer pairs. It covers conflicts arising from misinformation, differences over time, and semantic divergences. The authors organize their investigation around conflicts in retrieved knowledge, conflicts within encoded knowledge, and interactions between those two sources.

Controlled experiments examine twelve language-model instances from four model families, considering conflict types, model sizes, and effects at different stages. This design supplies a shared basis for investigating how models respond when their available information disagrees. The paper frames knowledge conflict as a major obstacle to trustworthy AI and offers the benchmark and analysis as resources for future training and development.
neurips-2024-texttt-conflictbank-a-bench.tldr: ConflictBank benchmarks how language models handle misinformation, temporal discrepancies, and semantic conflicts across retrieved and encoded knowledge.

paragraphs: VMamba adapts the Mamba state-space language model into a backbone for visual perception with linear time complexity. The central challenge is structural: language is naturally ordered as a sequence, while an image contains two-dimensional spatial relationships. A vision architecture must gather context without relying on a single natural sequence through the image.

The proposed backbone stacks Visual State-Space blocks built around a 2D Selective Scan module. This module traverses visual data along four scanning routes, collecting contextual information from different directions and perspectives. The routes connect one-dimensional selective scanning with the spatial organization of images, allowing the state-space approach to serve as a visual feature processor.

The authors develop a family of architectures and accelerate them through architectural and implementation improvements. Experiments report promising performance across diverse visual perception tasks and better input-scaling efficiency than benchmark models. These findings support the approach as a computationally efficient vision backbone, particularly when considering how processing demands grow with input size.
neurips-2024-vmamba-visual-state-space-m.tldr: VMamba adapts state-space modeling to vision using four-directional selective scans, achieving linear complexity and strong reported input-scaling efficiency.

paragraphs: Tourist photo collections show the same scene under changing appearances and temporary occlusions, complicating reconstruction and rendering from new viewpoints. Wild-GS adapts 3D Gaussian Splatting to these unconstrained collections while retaining its efficiency advantages. It aims to represent stable scene structure alongside the appearance differences between photographs.

Each Gaussian’s appearance incorporates inherent material attributes, image-level illumination and camera properties, and local reflectance variation. A triplane extracted from a reference image aligns pixel appearance features with local 3D Gaussians. This transfers fine appearance detail into the three-dimensional representation and accelerates training. Visibility maps help mitigate transient effects, while depth regularization constrains geometry.

The design brings appearance variation, temporary obstructions, and geometric structure into the reconstruction process through distinct components. Extensive experiments report state-of-the-art rendering performance and the highest training and inference efficiency among the compared techniques. These findings support efficient novel-view synthesis from photographs whose capture conditions are substantially less controlled than a consistent image collection.
neurips-2024-wild-gs-real-time-novel-vie.tldr: Wild-GS adapts Gaussian Splatting to changing appearances and temporary occlusions for efficient novel-view rendering from unconstrained photos.
